title: Simultaneous Equations
description: Solving two equations in two unknowns by elimination, substitution, and graphical methods.

notes.heading: Solving by Elimination
notes.body: Add or subtract equations to remove one variable. If coefficients of one variable match (or are opposites), add/subtract directly. If not, multiply one or both equations first. Example: 2x+3y=12 and 4x−3y=6 → add to get 6x=18 → x=3. Substitute back: 2(3)+3y=12 → y=2. Always verify in both equations.

notes.heading: Solving by Substitution
notes.body: Rearrange one equation to express one variable in terms of the other, then substitute into the second. Example: x+2y=8 and 3x−y=3 → from first: x=8−2y. Substitute: 3(8−2y)−y=3 → 24−7y=3 → y=3 → x=2. Efficient when one variable has coefficient 1.

notes.heading: Graphical Interpretation
notes.body: Each linear equation is a straight line. The solution is the intersection point (x, y). If lines are parallel (same gradient) → no solution. If lines are identical → infinitely many solutions.

notes.heading: Forming Equations from Word Problems
notes.body: Identify two unknowns (x, y) and translate each piece of information into an equation. Example: "Two apples and three bananas cost £1.60; one apple and five bananas cost £2.00." → 2x+3y=1.60, x+5y=2.00. Solve and interpret in context.

notes.heading: 📌 Definition
notes.body: A system of simultaneous linear equations is two or more linear equations that must be satisfied at the same time. A solution is an ordered pair $(x,y)$ that makes every equation in the system true.

notes.heading: 🔑 How it works
notes.body: To solve a system, reduce it to one equation with one unknown. Use elimination when the coefficients of one variable are equal or opposite, or can be made so by multiplication. Use substitution when one equation already has a variable with coefficient $1$ or is easy to rearrange. After finding the first value, substitute back to find the second.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example
notes.body:
Solve $$\begin{cases} 3x+2y=16 \\ 2x+3y=14 \end{cases}$$.

Multiply the first equation by $3$: $9x+6y=48$.
Multiply the second equation by $2$: $4x+6y=28$.
Subtract the new equations: $5x=20$, so $x=4$.
Substitute into the first original equation: $3(4)+2y=16$ → $12+2y=16$ → $y=2$.
Check in the second equation: $2(4)+3(2)=8+6=14$ ✓.

flashcards.definition: A set of two or more equations that share variables and must all be satisfied at the same time.
flashcards.example: 2x+y=7 and x−y=2; both true when x=3, y=1.

flashcards.definition: Add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable, then solve for the other.
Express one variable in terms of the other, then substitute into the second equation.
The coordinates (x, y) where two lines cross — the solution to the simultaneous equations.
When two lines are parallel (same gradient, different y-intercepts), there is no intersection.
Substitute x and y into BOTH original equations to verify.
When two equations describe the same line, every point on the line is a solution.
flashcards.example: $2x+y=4$ and $4x+2y=8$ are multiples of each other, so they share every point.

flashcards.definition: The numerical factor in front of a variable in a term.
flashcards.example: In $3x+2y=12$, the coefficient of $x$ is $3$ and of $y$ is $2$.

flashcards.definition: Rewrite a linear equation as $y=mx+c$ to read the gradient and y-intercept quickly.
flashcards.example: $2x+y=5$ becomes $y=-2x+5$, so the gradient is $-2$ and the y-intercept is $5$.

flashcards.definition: Pick elimination when coefficients match easily after multiplication; pick substitution when a variable is isolated or has coefficient $1$.
flashcards.example: $x+3y=7$ and $2x-y=4$ suit substitution because $x$ has coefficient $1$.

flashcards.definition: A system that has at least one solution — either one intersection point or infinitely many.
flashcards.example: $y=x+1$ and $y=2x-1$ meet at $(2,3)$, so the system is consistent.

flashcards.definition: After solving a word problem, verify that your answer makes sense with the original wording and units.
flashcards.example: If $x=2$ adults and $y=3$ children pay £9 and £5 each, $2(9)+3(5)=33$ must match the total given in the problem.

questions.stem: Solve: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
Solve by substitution: y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 14.
Two lines: y=x+2 and y=−x+6. Intersection?
Sum of two numbers is 20, difference is 6. Larger number?
y=3x−4 and y=3x+1. How many intersection points?
questions.explanation: Both have gradient 3 but different y-intercepts → parallel, no intersection.

questions.stem: Rectangle perimeter 28cm, length is 4cm more than width. Length?
Solve by substitution: x = 3y and 2x + y = 35.
A cinema: adult £9, child £5. 8 tickets total £56. How many adults?

questions.explanation: Multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second by $3$ to get $4x+6y=26$ and $15x-6y=12$. Adding gives $19x=38$, so $x=2$. Substitute into $2(2)+3y=13$ to get $y=3$.
Replace $y$ with $2x+3$ in the second equation: $4x-3(2x+3)=1$. This simplifies to $-2x-9=1$, so $x=-5$. Then $y=2(-5)+3=-7$.

questions.stem: Which pair of equations has no solution?
questions.explanation: Parallel lines have the same gradient but different y-intercepts. $y=3x+2$ and $y=3x-1$ both have gradient $3$, so they never meet.

questions.stem: Pens cost £1.50 and notebooks cost £2.50. Sarah buys 8 items for £16.00. How many notebooks?
questions.explanation: Let $p$ be pens and $n$ be notebooks. Then $p+n=8$ and $1.5p+2.5n=16$. Substitute $p=8-n$ to get $1.5(8-n)+2.5n=16$ → $12+n=16$ → $n=4$.

questions.stem: A system has infinitely many solutions. What must be true?
choices: The lines have the same gradient and different y-intercepts.
The lines have the same gradient and the same y-intercept.
The lines cross at exactly one point.
questions.explanation: Infinitely many solutions occur when both equations describe exactly the same line, which means equal gradients and equal y-intercepts.
